engine.title: The multibagger screen qualified nobody for four weeks
engine.body: Corrects what this entry said on 2026-08-27. It read ‘the scan is running on schedule’ and blamed the fixed list on cadence. The ledger says otherwise: the last multibagger row is 2026-08-01, while magic, magicmagic and ai_longterm — the same Saturday job, the same slot — all logged 2026-08-22. Twenty-six days, three Saturdays, nothing written.
engine.note: The screen is not broken. Run on 2026-08-27 it took 11 candidates and rejected 10 for R:R below 2.0 — CHENNPETRO 1.29, FLUOROCHEM 1.07, GLAXO 0.59, which needs a 63% win rate merely to break even. The defect was that a week qualifying nobody wrote nothing at all, so the page served the 1 August list as though it were current. The attempt is recorded either way now. The gate is NOT loosened: publishing a 0.59 R:R to keep the section busy is the exact trade this screen exists to refuse, and an empty week is a real result.

engine.title: Stop buying strength that has already run
engine.body: The 4H RSI ceiling for longs was 75. Splitting every closed trade by the RSI recorded at entry showed the engine bleeding above 65 and profitable below it. The ceiling is now 65.
engine.note: Holds in both halves of the sample and at every cut point tested (60, 65, 70), so it is not one lucky threshold. The threshold was still chosen from this sample, so treat the size as an upper bound.

engine.title: A break-even stop would not have helped
engine.body: The median losing trade was +1.44R in profit before it reversed, and 59% touched a full +1R first. That looks like an obvious fix: move the stop to entry once price pays 1R. Re-walking every trade bar by bar, with winners subject to the same rule, says otherwise.
engine.note: The first version of this test only altered losers, which guarantees a positive answer. Correcting it reversed the conclusion. Nothing tested cleared one standard error, so no stop rule was adopted.

engine.title: Trades were being closed at prices that never traded
engine.body: The grader had never resolved a single trade — an exception was being swallowed silently — leaving a fallback path that could book an exit at a bar from before the signal existed. Every closed trade was re-graded against bars that actually printed.
evidence: exits corrected to a real price
engine.note: This moved the headline number against me. It is published anyway, because the earlier number was not real. Pre-correction data is kept in the repo rather than deleted.

engine.title: A first target must pay back the risk
engine.body: T1 was whichever structural level sat nearest the entry, with no distance test. One signal shipped a T1 worth 0.19R against its own stop, printed beside an R:R of 2.41 quoted off T2. T1 must now return at least 1R.

chess.title: Tactics: The Pin
chess.body: A pin prevents a piece from moving because moving it would expose a more valuable piece behind it. Absolute pin = pinned to the king (piece cannot move legally). Relative pin = pinned to queen/rook (can move but it's a blunder). Identify pins in every position. Then exploit them.

book.author: Andy Grove
book.lesson: Grove invented OKRs at Intel in the 1970s. John Doerr brought them to Google in 1999. The structure: Objective (qualitative, inspirational — where do we want to go?) + Key Results (quantitative, measurable — how will we know we got there?). Rules: 3-5 OKRs per quarter. Each with 3-5 key results. They should be set at 60-70% achievable — if you always hit 100%, your targets are too easy. OKRs should be public so every team member can see how their work connects to company goals. The discipline of writing OKRs forces clarity on what actually matters and exposes misalignment between teams.
book.key_quote: What gets measured gets managed. What gets publicly committed to gets done.
book.action: Write one personal OKR for this quarter: Objective (where you want to be in your career by end of Q3) + 3 Key Results (how you'll know you got there).
crux: A manager's output is the output of their organisation plus the organisations they influence.
Managerial leverage = output ÷ time spent. Optimise for leverage, not effort.
Highest-leverage activities: training, and setting direction that many people then act on.
Production has three constraints everywhere: quality, cost, delivery time.
Inspect at the earliest, cheapest stage. Fixing at the end costs orders of magnitude more.
Indicators must come in pairs — one for output, one for the quality you might sacrifice for it.
Meetings are the medium of managerial work. A bad meeting is a process failure, not a waste of time in general.
One-on-ones are the highest-leverage meeting. The subordinate sets the agenda.
Decisions should be made at the lowest level with both knowledge and responsibility.
Aim for peer decision-making, then clear commitment even from dissenters.
Task-relevant maturity determines management style: low TRM needs structure, high TRM needs delegation.
Performance reviews exist to improve performance, not to rank people.
Three motivators when money is sufficient: competence, achievement, and self-actualisation.
learnings: Leverage is the only useful lens on how a manager spends an hour.
Paired indicators stop you optimising one number into a disaster.
Training your team is not overhead. It is the highest-return activity available.
Catch problems at the cheapest stage — the value-add curve is brutal.
examples: Grove's breakfast-factory model teaches limiting-step scheduling, quality gates, and capacity planning with eggs and toast.
Intel's move out of memory into microprocessors was executed through middle managers reallocating capacity before senior leadership formally decided.
Grove taught a class himself for years — one lecture, hundreds of managers, permanent leverage.
adapt: FP&A leverage: build the model once so 20 people read it right, instead of answering 20 questions.
Pair every metric: signals sent AND measured expectancy. One alone produced 180 alerts.
Inspect early — type-check and lint before commit, not after deploy.
In the Dubai role, one-on-ones with the business owners will be the highest-leverage hour of the week.

interview_tech.q: Sales per square foot is falling but total sales are rising. Diagnose it.
interview_tech.a: You are adding space faster than sales. That is not automatically wrong — new stores ramp, so a growth phase depresses the average mechanically. Split the estate: stores open more than 24 months versus less. If mature-store density is also falling, you have a genuine productivity problem — likely range, pricing, or footfall. If mature density is flat or up and only the blended number falls, it is a mix effect and it corrects as the new stores mature. Never let a board see the blended number alone.

interview_tech.q: Describe the difference between a cash flow forecast and a liquidity plan.
interview_tech.a: The forecast is your best estimate of receipts and payments. The liquidity plan is what you do if the forecast is wrong — committed facilities, uncommitted lines, the order in which you would draw them, what you would stop spending, and how quickly you could release working capital. Boards ask for the forecast; the CFO's real job is the plan. Stress it: what happens to cash if sales fall 20% for two quarters while committed rent and payroll continue.

interview_soft.q: How do you give feedback to someone more senior than you?
interview_soft.a: Ask permission, be specific, and stay on observable behaviour and its effect. 'Can I give you a reaction to how the numbers landed in that meeting? When the forecast changed without the bridge, the room stopped trusting the rest of the pack.' No adjectives about them, one concrete instance, and a suggestion. Then stop talking. Most people either avoid this entirely or overcorrect into confrontation.

interview_soft.q: How do you influence people who do not report to you?
interview_soft.a: Retail finance is almost entirely this — Buying, Operations and Retail Heads do not report to you. The answer is currency: work out what each function is measured on and frame your ask in their terms. A buyer cares about sell-through and margin, not about your working capital target — so bring them the SKU-level analysis showing which lines tie up cash without turning. Give people the analysis they cannot build themselves, and influence follows. Name a specific instance and the outcome.

cfo_field.q: The controller who never leaves the close never becomes CFO.
cfo_field.a: The job you are promoted out of is 'the person who produces the numbers'. The job you are promoted into is 'the person who decides what to do about them'. If your calendar is 70% close, reconciliation and audit prep, you are demonstrating that you are excellent at the job you already have. Push the close down: a well-run retail group closes in 5 working days, and every day you shave buys back roughly 12 days a year of capacity to spend on decisions instead of production.

cfo_field.q: The Gulf pays for scarcity, not for years.
cfo_field.a: Salary in the region tracks the intersection of skills, not the length of the CV. CA plus genuine FP&A plus retail plus a system implementation is a much rarer combination than any one of them is deep. If you are negotiating, the leverage is in naming the intersection, not in listing the years. And check the structure: basic versus allowances changes gratuity, which is calculated on basic salary alone.

lichess_games.analysis: Focus on early central tension: after 1.e4 e5 2.Nc3, develop with …Nf6 instead of …Bc5; avoid the passive 3…d6 line that lets White dominate the center. Strengthen your opening by 0.3 % (≈1‑2 ELO) per game.

Focus on early piece activity: after 1.d4 c5 2.d5 e6, develop Nf3 before committing to c4; avoid passive moves like a3, and aim for timely …cxd5 exchanges to free your queenside. This will give you clearer plans and reduce cramped positions.

Strengthen your opening: after 1.d4 d5 2.c4, play …e6 instead of …c5; avoid early queen moves and develop knights before committing pawns.Improve opening: after 1.d4 d5 2.c4, choose …e6 over …c5, develop knights first, keep queen tucked, avoid unnecessary pawn pushes.
lichess_games.standout: 3 blunders in one game. The result is noise; the error count is the signal.

lichess_games.analysis: Focus on early pawn structure: avoid 2…d5? after 1.e4 e5 2.Nc3; instead play 2…Nc6, preserving central tension and preventing the quick 3.Bc4 Bxc4 4.Qh5+.
lichess_games.standout: Over in 10 moves — decided in the opening, so the opening is what to study.

lichess_summary.session_summary: Your Vienna Game is a fatal joke—two wins don’t prove mastery, they expose a reckless reliance on surprise rather than substance. Stop treating the opening as a crutch and drill the underlying pawn structures, piece coordination, and end‑game transitions until you can win from any position, not just the Vienna’s gimmicks. From now on, spend every training hour on concrete calculation drills and a systematic opening repertoire; if you can’t convert a standard Sicilian or Caro‑Kann, you’ll never climb beyond 1500.

lichess_puzzle.tip: Calculate 3 moves deep before touching a piece.
